source.title: FRoG: Evaluating Fuzzy Reasoning of Generalized Quantifiers in Large Language Models
source.authors: Yi-Yuan Li; Shichao Sun; Pengfei Liu

record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps parameter sizes and measures benchmark accuracy rather than held-out pretraining loss, testing whether downstream performance scales predictably on a different task.
record.gate_note: The reported scaling results are FRoG task accuracy versus model size. The paper also reports comparisons among masking tasks and model variants, but they are not separately included unless they bear on downstream scaling.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates released checkpoints of 15 model families on a new fuzzy-reasoning benchmark (FRoG) and asks whether accuracy improves with parameter count. That is a new setting with a result on V6. It fits no law, measures no loss and trains no models, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that FRoG is hard for current LLMs, with all models below 50% accuracy. They find inverse scaling, which they define as under 1 point of gain from scaling, in 8 of 15 families. Continued pretraining on math or code, instruction tuning and alignment do not reliably help. Strong precise math reasoning does not imply success on fuzzy reasoning.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures multiple-choice benchmark accuracy across existing model sizes, not held-out pretraining loss or training compute; it does not fit scaling exponents or perform compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Difficulty mode (Easy versus Hard), model family, base versus instruction-tuned or DPO variant, and size range affect the reported scaling pattern.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger models lose more accuracy when moving from the precise mask_percent task to the fuzzy mask_quant task: 16.9% average drop versus 6.8% for models under 10B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gains from scale on precise numeric reasoning transfer less to fuzzy quantifier reasoning as models grow.

record.problems: Accuracy is measured on one constructed fuzzy-reasoning benchmark, not held-out language-modeling loss. Scaling trends are described across available checkpoints without fitted exponents or uncertainty estimates. The authors note the masking protocol may differ from real-world fuzzy reasoning and that generalized-quantifier reasoning is only part of fuzzy reasoning.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports individual accuracy values for many models and masking strategies in Table 3 and Figures 3–8. These were not separately extracted; the rows retain the explicit scaling trends and conditions that bear most directly on V6.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss; no power-law fit.
No shape or architecture comparison at fixed size.
No other modalities or training regimes.

Predictability from pretraining loss, and any fitted trend or forecast. Only the direction of the accuracy change across released checkpoints is reported. Families differ in data and training, so scale is confounded with other factors.

missing.what: Inverse-scaling checks for the Mislead and X% masking tasks, by family and difficulty. The rows cover only the Mask task.
Declines with size in families no row covers: Yi-Chat Hard 23.4→20.0 (6B→34B), and CodeLlama 34B→70B collapse 22.6→7.5. The authors attribute the CodeLlama collapse to code-style outputs.

record.verdict_notes: Table 3 pairs appear to be Hard/Easy (Easy is higher, matching the text). The paper's 'inverse scaling' mostly means a plateau rather than a decline, so several rows were downgraded from reversed to partial. The comparisons are across heterogeneous released checkpoints with no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether loss laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its growth with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and architecture at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
No relation to pretraining loss is measured; results concern FRoG accuracy across parameter sizes, not predictability across downstream tasks generally.
No fitted loss exponents, compute-optimal split, or sensitivity to fitting choices is evaluated.

rows.check: The paper defines 'inverse scaling' as under 1 point of gain from scaling (Table 4), not a decline. Table 3 Hard values are 22.5/23.8/24.0 for 7B/13B/70B: a small gain, so partial, not reversed.

rows.note: The paper names Llama-2 among instruction-tuned models with inverse scaling in Easy mode.
rows.check: Llama-2-Chat Easy is 26.8/26.6/31.9 (Table 3). That is flat from 7B to 13B, then +5.3 at 70B. Not an overall reversal.

rows.check: Llama-2-Chat Hard is 24.3/25.6/25.3: a small gain, then flat. Under the paper's <1-point definition this is weak scaling, not reversal.

rows.note: The paper also says performance saturates at 7 billion parameters or larger and gains diminish after 14 billion parameters.

relationships.condition: Llama-2 base (Easy), Qwen-1.5 base, Llama-3 base and Instruct, Tulu-2 base on the Mask task
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises with size in these families, e.g. Llama-3-Instruct Easy goes 22.8→42.9 (R1, R5, R8, R9, R10).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased with size across the specified families, including Llama-3-Instruct Easy from 22.8 to 42.9.

relationships.condition: Llama-2 Hard (base and chat), Llama-2-Chat Easy, Tulu-2-DPO, Qwen-1.5-Chat at 7B and above, and the 8/15-family aggregate
relationships.reason: Gains are under about 1 point per scale step or saturate. The improvement is weak or non-monotone rather than predictable (R2, R3, R4, R6, R7, R11, R12).
relationships.display_finding: Gains stayed below about one point per size step or saturated in the tested Llama-2, Llama-2-Chat, Tulu-2-DPO, and Qwen-1.5-Chat settings, with some nonmonotonic trajectories.

relationships.reason: Accuracy falls with size: Hard 21.4→15.5 and Easy 19.1→18.3 (R6, Table 3).
relationships.display_finding: Hard accuracy fell from 21.4 to 15.5 and Easy accuracy from 19.1 to 18.3.
